title: Cell birth and death rates of tissues: turnover, stem-cell pools and age effects for hepatocytes, cardiomyocytes, skeletal muscle, epidermis, gut, bone, red cells and neurons, with plant leaf and fine-root turnover (task 3019, integration gap CG-15)
source: Sender and Milo 2021 (PDF read), Bergmann 2009 and 2015, Heinke 2022, Michalopoulos 2007, Spalding 2013, Sorrells 2018, Bhardwaj 2006, Verdijk 2007, Pawlikowski 2015, Eriksen 2010, Clarke 2008, Manolagas 2000, Catlin 2011, Pang 2011, Higgins and Mahadevan 2010, Barker 2007, Alcolea and Jones 2014, Clayton 2007, Gill and Jackson 2000 (PDF read), McCormack 2015, Reich 2004, Chave 2010, Monteiro and Korner 2013, Wright 2004. Most were abstracts or page text read through fetch tools; where a figure comes from a search summary the Note column says so. Rows marked 'my arithmetic' or 'my conversion' are derived from other rows.
rows: Total cell turnover of the human body
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau

Printed as 0.33 +/- 0.02 x 10^12 cells per day (about 4 million per second); Low and High are value -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic). 86% blood cells, almost all of the rest gut cells; erythrocytes, neutrophils and gut epithelium are about 96% of it. Cells of 30 trillion in the body; the whole count turns over in about 80 days.
Total cellular mass turnover of the human body
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau

Printed as 80 +/- 20 g per day (wet mass of cells that die or are shed), about 0.1% of body mass or 0.2% of cellular mass per day; blood about 40% and gut epithelium about 40% of it. Fat and muscle cells are about 75% of cellular mass but only about 5% of the mass turnover. Whole cells only, not protein turnover inside living cells.
Share of cellular mass turnover from fat and muscle cells
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau

Printed as 'around 5%' for adipocytes and muscle cells together, against about 75% of cellular mass. The paper warns that radioisotope-label estimates for muscle 'tend to indicate nuclei turnover rather than whole-cell turnover'; no whole-cell lifespan for skeletal muscle is given.
Share of body cells never replaced (most brain neurons and eye-lens cells)
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau
Printed as about 0.5% of cells, calculated by the authors from two cited sources; the paper says 'complete turnover never happens'.
Lifespan assumed for stem cells in the census
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau
The authors 'assumed a lifespan equal to the age of the reference person' for stem cells (a convention, not a measurement). The paper gives no rate for stem-pool output.
Mean lifespan of circulating red blood cells

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; average of three models fitted to 2H2O labelling data
Printed as 116 +/- 3 d; Low and High are -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic). Older radioactive-label estimates are said to be biased by toxicity.
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; 94 +/- 4 pg per cell
Printed as 2.1 +/- 0.1 x 10^11 cells per day, 20 +/- 1 g per day; a check from marrow progenitors (3.1 +/- 0.5 x 10^11 cells) is described but its result is not printed in the text read.
Red blood cell lifespan in children, and in women
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; children

Printed as 60 to 80 d in children against 120 d in adults; women also have shorter lifespans and pregnancy shortens it more (no number given in the text read). Value is the middle of the range (my arithmetic).
Higgins and Mahadevan 2010, PNAS 107:20587; master-equation model fitted to hospital blood counts; abstract read
Printed as 'removed after about 120 days, triggered by an unknown signal'. The abstract gives no production rate.
Replication interval of human haematopoietic stem cells in vivo
Catlin et al 2011, Blood 117:4460-4466; X-chromosome ratio change with age in women, checked two ways; abstract read

Printed as about once every 40 weeks (range 25 to 50), which is 1.3 divisions per year (my conversion). Models reproduced transplant data and suggest stem-cell numbers rise from birth to adolescence and then level off; no absolute number given.
Haematopoietic stem cell frequency and output with age
Pang et al 2011, PNAS 108:20012-20017; human marrow, young donors 20 to 35 y against healthy donors over 65; flow cytometry and mouse transplants; abstract text relayed by a search summary

No number. Aged stem cells are more frequent among CD34+ cells, less quiescent and myeloid-biased; lymphoid progenitors decline while myeloid progenitors are maintained. So the pool grows with age; the output mix, not the total, changes.
Neutrophil lifespan in blood, and post-mitotic transit time

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; from half-lives of 13, 16 and 19 h in the 2H2O study of Lahoz-Beneytez et al

Printed as 0.9 +/- 0.1 d in blood and 5.7 +/- 0.1 d post-mitotic transit in marrow; total turnover 6 +/- 1 x 10^10 cells (18 +/- 4 g) per day. Old labels had given half-lives under 7 h and the paper rejects them.

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; two to three methods weighted by patients from a meta-analysis
Printed as 5.3 +/- 1.7 d; 1.2 +/- 0.2 x 10^11 cells; 2 +/- 1 x 10^10 cells (19 +/- 8 g) per day. Low and High are -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic). The paper's introduction gives '3-5 d for gut epithelia'.
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau
Printed as 3.4 +/- 0.5 d; 5.6 +/- 2 x 10^10 cells; 1.7 +/- 0.6 x 10^10 cells (14 +/- 6 g) per day. Low and High are -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic).
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau
Printed as 13 +/- 9 d; 1.3 +/- 0.9 x 10^9 cells (1.1 +/- 0.7 g) per day. Low and High are -/+ 1 s.e. (my arithmetic).
Intestinal stem cells and their output
Barker et al 2007, Nature 449:1003-1007; mouse small intestine and colon, inducible Cre lineage tracing; abstract read

Lgr5-positive cells at the crypt base generated all epithelial lineages over 60 days. The abstract says the intestinal lining renews faster than any other adult mammalian tissue and that 'four to six' stem cells at the +4 position were the belief before. No cell-cycle time or stem-cell count for humans is in the abstract; the 2014 review (Barker, Nat Rev Mol Cell Biol 15:19-33) abstract gives none either.
Change of intestinal stem-cell output with age
Sender and Milo 2021 (children's gut lifespan from mouse data); Barker 2007
No human number found. The census says children probably have a shorter intestinal lifespan, 'shown for mice', and gives no adult age trend.
Lifespan of epidermal keratinocytes (basal layer to loss of viable cells)

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; main values from 1970s and 1980s labelling-index studies; the stratum corneum (dead corneocytes) is excluded

Printed as a range of 25 to 38 d, whose average the paper took as the reference; Value is the midpoint (my arithmetic). 1.2 +/- 0.3 x 10^11 nucleated keratinocytes; turnover 3.7 +/- 0.9 x 10^9 cells (3.1 +/- 0.8 g) per day. Psoriasis shortens the lifespan substantially.
Division rate of mouse tail epidermal progenitors, and of slow-cycling stem cells
divisions per week (progenitors); about once per 3 months (slow-cycling)
Alcolea and Jones 2014, Cold Spring Harb Perspect Med 4:a015206 (review, first 100,000 characters read); mouse tail epidermis

The review says mouse tail progenitors 'divide once a week' on average, that the Figure 2 legend gives about once every 3 months for stem cells, and a model uses 10 to 12 weeks for slow-cycling cells. No division rate for human epidermis, and no age trend, is given.
Clayton et al 2007, Nature 446:185-189; mouse tail epidermis, genetic labelling for up to one year; abstract text relayed by a search summary

Clone-size data fit a single progenitor type that divides to give two, one or no cycling daughters in proportions that keep the tissue level; the abstract says stem cells and transit-amplifying cells dividing at different rates cannot give the observed scaling. A commentary summary adds that stem cells are quiescent unless the skin is wounded. No number.
Heinke et al 2022, Cell Systems 13:499-507; carbon-14 birth dating of liver from donors aged 20 to 84; abstract read through Europe PMC

Printed as 'under 3 years' on average. Diploid hepatocytes have more than 7-fold higher annual birth rates than polyploid hepatocytes; switching between ploidy states is limited in homeostasis. The paper is not in PMC; the next two rows come from the TU Dresden press release of 31 May 2022.
Turnover of diploid hepatocytes, and persistence of polyploid ones
turnovers per year (diploid); polyploid up to about 10 years
Heinke et al 2022 as reported in the TU Dresden press release (search summary, release not opened)

Release says most hepatocytes, which are diploid, turn over about once a year, and a subpopulation with more DNA sets can persist up to a decade, and that ageing does not appear to affect liver renewal. Not read in the paper itself.
Human hepatocyte lifespan from direct measurement, per census
Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau

Sender and Milo list hepatocytes with alveolar cells as cell types where 'the only available data were measurements in rodents'; the rodent lifespan is used only for the upper bound on extra turnover (with lung, 17 g per day), not as a human value.
Hepatocytes entering DNA synthesis after two-thirds partial hepatectomy
% of hepatocytes (first round); more than 95% within 48 h
Michalopoulos 2007, J Cell Physiol 213:286-300 (review, first 100,000 of 249,503 characters read); rat and mouse

Printed as one round of DNA synthesis in 60% of hepatocytes, peaking at 24 h in rat and about 36 h in mouse, a smaller second round that restores the original number, more than 95% of hepatocytes in cell proliferation during 48 h, and a small apoptosis wave at the end that corrects overshoot. A two-thirds resection leaves one-third of hepatocytes.
Time to restore liver weight after two-thirds partial hepatectomy
days (rat and mouse); human 8 to 15 days
Printed as 'complete within 5-7 days after surgery' in rats and mice and '8-15 days in humans'. Value is the midpoint of the rodent range (my arithmetic).

Printed as 'proliferation of mature adult hepatocytes'; 'Liver histology does not contain any cells that appear to be full-time, committed, stem cells'; biliary-derived oval cells take over only when hepatocytes cannot proliferate. Quiescence of the normal liver is kept by signals that the review discusses without a rate.
Donor liver volume regrowth after right-lobe donation
% of pre-operative volume of the remnant at day 30 (88.5% of whole-liver volume)
Kwon et al 2003, Yonsei Med J, living donors; and Humar et al (3 months 78.6% of ideal volume, 1 year 83.3% of baseline); figures relayed by a search summary, the page loaded blank

Marked open: neither page was read. The relay says the remnant went from 687.8 cm3 to 81.4% of its pre-operative size by day 30, whole liver to 88.5% of the pre-operative volume, with liver function recovered by day 30.
Annual turnover of human cardiomyocytes, from age 25 to age 75
Bergmann et al 2009, Science 324:98-102; carbon-14 from nuclear tests in DNA of left-ventricle cells; abstract read

Printed as 1% turning over annually at age 25 falling gradually to 0.45% at age 75, with fewer than 50% of cardiomyocytes exchanged in a normal life span. Rates are model outputs (best fit an inverse-linear fall). Value is the mean of the two ends (my arithmetic).
Cardiomyocyte renewal in adulthood, and non-myocyte turnover in the heart
Bergmann et al 2015, Cell 161:1566-1575; carbon-14 birth dating, human heart; abstract read

Printed as: cardiomyocyte number set perinatally and stable for life; exchange highest in early childhood and falling to under 1% per year in adulthood; endothelial cells above 15% per year throughout life; mesenchymal cells under 4% per year in adulthood. No separate figures for ages 20 or 75 in the abstract.
Satellite cells per muscle fibre, young against elderly men
cells per type II fibre (young 0.080, elderly 0.044)
Verdijk et al 2007, Am J Physiol Endocrinol Metab 292:E151-E157; vastus lateralis biopsies, 8 men aged 76 +/- 1 y and 8 aged 20 +/- 1 y; Pax7; abstract read

Printed as 0.044 +/- 0.003 against 0.080 +/- 0.007 per type II fibre (P under 0.01), about 45% lower (my calculation); type I fibres similar. Other studies cited elsewhere found no such difference (not read). Satellite cell turnover or division rate in humans is not given.
Share of adult mouse muscle fibres that took up satellite-cell nuclei
% of hindlimb fibres over a 6-month chase (tibialis anterior 78, 60, 20, 20% at 4, 8, 12, 27 weeks; diaphragm 80 to 95%)
Pawlikowski et al 2015, Skeletal Muscle 5:42; mouse lineage tracing with tamoxifen; PMC text read through a page-fetch summary

Printed ranges as listed; hindlimb fusion reaches a steady state by about 12 weeks of age. Myonuclear turnover is inferred, not measured: constant satellite-cell and myonuclear numbers with high fusion imply loss of nuclei 'unless myonuclei accumulate at the myotendonous junctions'. Mouse; the summary found inconsistent values in the paper (tibialis anterior about 15% or 20%).
Lifespan of human myonuclei or muscle fibres
Searched: carbon-14, label and lineage studies; Sender and Milo 2021

No measured human value was read. Sender and Milo warn that label-based muscle estimates reflect nuclei, not whole cells. A search summary relayed a mean myonuclear age of about 15 years in intercostal muscle of two people, from a review that was not opened, so it is not recorded as a number.
Duration of a remodelling cycle in cancellous bone
days (normal about 200; 100 in thyrotoxicosis or primary hyperparathyroidism; over 1,000 in low-turnover states)
Eriksen 2010, Rev Endocr Metab Disord 11:219-227 (review, PMC text read through a page-fetch summary)
Printed as 'lasts about 200 days in normal bone', 'as short as 100 days' and 'exceed 1,000 days' after bisphosphonate treatment or in myxoedema. Resorption median 30 to 40 d; formation about 150 d.
Duration of a remodelling cycle in cortical bone
Printed as 'with a median of 120 days'.
Time for the cancellous bone surface to be completely remodelled
Printed as 'completely remodeled over a period of 2 years' (so about half the surface per year, my inference; the review gives no per-year percentage for the skeleton).
Clarke 2008, Clin J Am Soc Nephrol 3 Suppl 3:S131-S139 (review, PMC text read through a page-fetch summary)

Printed as '2 to 3%/yr'; trabecular turnover is faster but the review gives no number. Resorption 'approximately 2 to 4 wk', formation 'approximately 4 to 6 mo'; 50 to 70% of osteoblasts undergo apoptosis at the end of formation. Value is the midpoint (my arithmetic).
Depth of resorption lacuna, young against older people

Printed as '60 in young individuals and 40 um in older individuals'; the review says osteoclastic resorption is augmented in old bone and that in osteoporosis the osteoblast cannot refill the lacuna. No numeric rate change with age or menopause.
Manolagas 2000, Endocr Rev 21:115-137 (review; abstract text relayed by a search summary; full text paywalled); Eriksen 2010; Clarke 2008

No lifespan in days or weeks was read: Eriksen and Clarke give none, and the Manolagas abstract describes birth and apoptosis rates as central to bone balance without numbers (a BioNumbers entry points to its Table 1, whose value text did not load).
New neurons added in the adult human hippocampus
Spalding et al 2013, Cell 153:1219-1227; carbon-14 in DNA of neuron nuclei from people born around the bomb tests; abstract read

Printed as 700 new neurons per hippocampus per day, 1.75% per year of the renewing fraction with a modest decline with age, a renewing subpopulation of about one third of hippocampal neurons. Disputed by Sorrells et al 2018 (next row).
Hippocampal neurogenesis across childhood and adulthood
Sorrells et al 2018, Nature 555:377-381; 59 post-mortem and surgical hippocampi; abstract text relayed by a search summary

Printed as neurogenesis 'does not continue, or is extremely rare, in the adult human brain'; the relay adds 23-fold fewer new neurons from age 1 to 7 and a further 5-fold fall by 13. The two papers conflict; the authorities are named, not reconciled.
Neurogenesis in the human neocortex in adulthood
Bhardwaj et al 2006, PNAS 103:12564-12568; carbon-14 and BrdU in cortical tissue; abstract read

Printed as 'neurons in the human cerebral neocortex are not generated in adulthood at detectable levels', generated perinatally; non-neuronal cells do turn over. The 0 is 'not detectable', not proven absent.
Energy to make the protein of new cells

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; theory and experiment cited, mainly bacteria and yeast

Printed as 4.5 to 5.3 kJ per g protein (6 to 7 ATP per amino acid at -80 kJ per mol); Value is the midpoint (my arithmetic). About 15 g protein per day in new cells (80 g wet, 70% water, 60% of dry mass protein), 16 to 19 kcal per day, about 1% of whole-body resting rate and about 3% of the gut's; marrow 8 to 9 kcal and gut 7 to 8 kcal per day. The authors treat it as a sanity check.
Cellular mass accumulation against adult homeostatic turnover
% of body mass per day (newborn); adult turnover about 0.1%

Sender and Milo 2021, Nature Medicine 27:45-48 (PDF text read); reference adult, 70 kg, 170 cm; lifespan is time from last division to death; turnover beta = n / tau; mass accumulation in Extended Data Fig. 4

Printed as a newborn gaining about 30 g per day (about 1% per day) in the first 3 months, a third-trimester fetus 10 to 25 g of cellular mass per day (about 1%), against adult turnover of 80 g per day (about 0.1% of body mass); from 9 months of age the relative rate of mass accumulation is below an adult man's turnover.
Turnover of whole tree root systems
Gill and Jackson 2000, New Phytologist 147:13-31; database of 190 published studies; turnover = annual root production as a fraction of maximum live root standing crop; PDF text read
Printed as the slowest class, 10% annually.
Gill and Jackson 2000, New Phytologist 147:13-31; database of 190 published studies; turnover = annual root production as a fraction of maximum live root standing crop; PDF text read
Gill and Jackson 2000, New Phytologist 147:13-31; database of 190 published studies; turnover = annual root production as a fraction of maximum live root standing crop; PDF text read
Gill and Jackson 2000, New Phytologist 147:13-31; database of 190 published studies; turnover = annual root production as a fraction of maximum live root standing crop; PDF text read
Printed as 56% for roots of 5 mm or less pooled over all latitudes; wetland fine roots 55%. Temperature explains little (r2 = 0.17); Q10 1.4.
Root turnover by latitude zone (graminoids, shrubs and tree fine roots)
% per year (high latitude 13, temperate 40, tropical about 73)
Gill and Jackson 2000, New Phytologist 147:13-31; database of 190 published studies; turnover = annual root production as a fraction of maximum live root standing crop; PDF text read

Printed as 13% at high latitude, 40% in temperate zones and 'nearly 73%' in tropical zones, as a fraction of maximum standing crop per year. Value is the tropical figure. The per-group tropical values (tree fine roots, grasses) are in Figure 5 only, which the text extraction does not give as numbers.
Tropical grassland fine-root turnover and tropical tree fine-root turnover separately
Gill and Jackson 2000, New Phytologist 147:13-31; database of 190 published studies; turnover = annual root production as a fraction of maximum live root standing crop; PDF text read

Not found as numbers: the paper reports only the pooled tropical figure in text and shows the split in Figure 5 (axis 0 to 1.0 per year); the order is stated as grasslands = tree fine roots = wetlands > shrublands > whole tree root system within each zone.
Forest fine-root turnover by diameter class
per year (0 to 1 mm 1.2; 0 to 3 or 0 to 5 mm 0.52; 0 to 10 mm 0.10; mean of all classes 0.56)
Gill and Jackson 2000, New Phytologist 147:13-31; database of 190 published studies; turnover = annual root production as a fraction of maximum live root standing crop; PDF text read
Printed as listed; most studies used 0 to 3 or 0 to 5 mm. 'The inconsistency in defining fine roots' is named as a barrier to comparison.
Gill and Jackson 2000, New Phytologist 147:13-31; database of 190 published studies; turnover = annual root production as a fraction of maximum live root standing crop; PDF text read
Printed as 1.4 for forest roots of 5 mm or less, 1.6 for grassland and all fine roots, 1.9 for shrublands; no relation to precipitation once temperature is in the model.
Share of terrestrial net primary production in fine-root production and turnover
McCormack et al 2015, New Phytologist 207:505-518 (review); abstract read through Europe PMC

Printed as 22%, about 30% lower than estimates with a single fine-root pool; the review proposes an order-based or a two-pool (short-lived absorptive, longer-lived transport) split. Full text subscription-only, not read; no per-biome turnover per year in the abstract.
Leaf lifespan of Amazonian Tierra Firme forest trees by light
years (sunlit canopy 1.6, small gaps 1.9, deep shade 3.2)
Reich et al 2004, Ecological Monographs 74:3-23; San Carlos de Rio Negro, Venezuela; more than 40,000 leaves of 1,445 trees of 23 evergreen species; abstract read
Printed as listed. Caatinga forest 2.5, 3.4 and 4.2 years in the same order. Leaf production, mortality and lifespan showed no link to the mild dry season (aseasonal).
Leaf lifespan of tropical tree species of other communities
years (disturbed open sites median 0.7, 7 species; infertile Bana 1.9, 5 species; tall primary forest high-light canopy 2.0, 6 species)
Reich et al 2004, Ecological Monographs 74:3-23; San Carlos de Rio Negro, Venezuela; more than 40,000 leaves of 1,445 trees of 23 evergreen species; abstract read
Printed as listed; a 1991 paper from the same site found a 30-fold range of leaf lifespan among 23 species (relayed by a search summary, not opened).
Annual leaf replacement of tropical forest canopy trees, as one over the lifespan
per year (1.6 y gives 0.63; 4.2 y gives 0.24; 0.7 y gives 1.43)
Reich et al 2004, Ecological Monographs 74:3-23; San Carlos de Rio Negro, Venezuela; more than 40,000 leaves of 1,445 trees of 23 evergreen species; abstract read
My arithmetic (1 / lifespan), a steady-state leaf-population turnover; not printed by the source.
Leaf litterfall of tropical South American old-growth forest
Mg dry mass per hectare per year
Chave et al 2010, Biogeosciences 7:43-55; 81 sites; HTML page read through a fetch summary

Printed as 5.74 +/- 1.83 (mean +/- s.d.), 71% of total litterfall of 8.61 +/- 1.91 (old growth; secondary 8.01 +/- 3.41; white sand 5.42 +/- 1.91). Low and High are -/+ 1 s.d. (my arithmetic). Seasonality rises with rainfall seasonality; annual total not related to annual rainfall.
Leaf lifespan of a tall tussock grass of the tropical Andes
Monteiro and Korner 2013, Alpine Botany 123:13-20; Festuca orthophylla at 4,250 m, Sajama, Bolivia; abstract read
Printed as 141 and 169 days. This is a high-altitude C3 grass, not a lowland tropical or C4 grass; value is the midpoint (my arithmetic), about two leaf replacements a year.
Leaf lifespan of lowland tropical and savanna grasses
Searched: standard web searches for tropical or savanna grass leaf longevity

No lowland tropical grass value was found: results were for temperate forage grasses (phyllochron in degree-days, not read), savanna shrubs (66 to 283 days, from a snippet, not opened) and the Andean tussock above.
Range of leaf lifespan across the worldwide leaf economics spectrum
Wright et al 2004, Nature 428:821-827; 2,548 species at 175 sites; abstract text relayed by a search summary

The abstract names a global 'quick to slow' gradient in leaf return on nutrient and dry-mass investment, independent of growth form and biome; no lifespan range was in the text read and the full paper was not opened.
